title: Monotonic Stack
summary: Maintaining an ordered stack while scanning so every "next greater/smaller" style question resolves in one linear pass instead of a nested loop.

slides.markdown:
A **monotonic stack** keeps its elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order at all times, by popping anything that would break that order before pushing a new element. That one discipline turns an entire family of "next greater," "next smaller," and "largest rectangle" problems from O(n²) nested loops into a single O(n) pass.

The deep idea, previewed in the previous topic: an element only gets popped once its answer is **settled for good** — once you know its next-greater (or next-smaller), nothing that happens later can change that answer, so it's safe to discard it from further consideration. Every problem in this topic is a variation on exploiting that settled-once property.

slides.subTitle: Popping an element only once its answer is settled for good
slides.markdown:
Scan left to right maintaining a stack of indices whose next-greater element hasn't been found yet. When a new element arrives bigger than the stack's top, that top element's search is **over** — the new element is its answer, so pop it and record the answer, then check the new top against the same new element.

The key property: once an element gets popped this way, it never needs to be examined again. Its answer is permanently settled. That's what makes the total work O(n) despite the inner `while` loop: across the whole scan, each element is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the total number of pop operations across the entire algorithm is bounded by n, not by n per outer iteration.

slides.sectionTitle: Next greater element in one O(n) pass
slides.markdown:
```python
def next_greater(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    answer = [-1] * n
    stack = []  # holds indices, values decreasing bottom to top
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < nums[i]:
            answer[stack.pop()] = nums[i]
        stack.append(i)
    return answer
```

Each index is pushed once and popped at most once across the whole run, so despite the nested-looking `while`, total work is O(n). Indices left on the stack at the end have no next-greater element (their answer stays -1).

"How many days until a warmer temperature?" is next-greater-element with the **distance**, not the value, as the answer.

```python
def daily_temperatures(temps):
    n = len(temps)
    answer = [0] * n
    stack = []  # indices with temps in decreasing order
    for i, t in enumerate(temps):
        while stack and temps[stack[-1]] < t:
            j = stack.pop()
            answer[j] = i - j  # days until warmer
        stack.append(i)
    return answer
```

Same algorithm, same O(n) bound — only the payload computed on each pop changed from "the value" to "the index gap." Recognizing that a new problem is the same skeleton with a different payload is the actual transferable skill here.

slides.sectionTitle: Why you push indices, not values
slides.markdown:
Nearly every monotonic-stack problem needs more than just the value at the top — it needs **where** that value was, to compute a distance (daily temperatures), a width (largest rectangle in a histogram), or to look up other per-position data (like a separate prefix array).

Pushing values alone throws away exactly the information most of these problems need. Pushing indices costs nothing extra — you can always recover the value with `nums[i]` — while keeping every downstream computation that needs position available. The rare exception is a problem that only ever needs the value itself and never a distance or width; even then, pushing indices is harmless, so it's the safe default habit.

For each bar, the largest rectangle using that bar's height extends left and right until hitting a shorter bar. A monotonic (increasing) stack of indices finds both boundaries in one pass.

```python
def largest_rectangle(heights):
    stack = []  # indices, heights increasing bottom to top
    max_area = 0
    for i, h in enumerate(heights + [0]):  # sentinel 0 flushes the stack
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            width = i if not stack else i - stack[-1] - 1
            max_area = max(max_area, height * width)
        stack.append(i)
    return max_area
```

When a bar is popped because a shorter one arrived, the popped bar's rectangle spans from just after the new stack top to the current index — both boundaries fall out of the stack's remaining contents for free.

slides.sectionTitle: Forgetting to flush the remaining stack
slides.markdown:
```python
# BUG: never processes bars still on the stack when input ends
for i, h in enumerate(heights):  # no sentinel appended
    while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= h:
        ...
    stack.append(i)
return max_area  # any bars still on the stack were never resolved
```

If the input ends while bars are still on the stack (common when the histogram is non-decreasing, so nothing ever triggers a pop), their rectangles never get computed — including, often, the single largest one, since a monotonically increasing histogram's biggest rectangle is usually anchored at its tallest, last-pushed bar.

The standard fix is appending a **sentinel** value of 0 (or negative infinity) to the end of the input before scanning, which is guaranteed to be less than or equal to everything still on the stack and forces every remaining bar to be popped and resolved.

slides.subTitle: With a monotonic stack, and where two pointers live instead
slides.markdown:
Trapping rain water — how much water sits above a bar array after rain — can be solved with a monotonic (decreasing) stack of indices: when a taller bar arrives, the popped bar becomes a **basin floor**, bounded on the left by the new stack top and on the right by the arriving bar, and you add the trapped volume at that floor.

This works and is O(n), but it isn't the leanest solution — a two-pointer approach (tracking a running max from each side) solves the same problem in O(n) time and O(1) space, without a stack at all. That two-pointer version is covered in the `two-pointers-sliding-window` group, which is where this exact problem's canonical solution lives; it's mentioned here only to show the monotonic-stack framing is *a* valid lens, not the only or best one for every problem shaped like this.

slides.sectionTitle: Monotonic stack vs brute-force nested loop
slides.subTitle: Turning O(n²) into O(n) by never re-examining an element
slides.markdown:
| | Brute force | Monotonic stack |
|---|---|---|
| Time | O(n²) | O(n) |
| Space | O(1) | O(n) worst case |
| Core idea | re-scan from every index | each element pushed and popped at most once, total |
| When brute force is fine | n is small, or this runs once | n large, or runs in a hot loop |

The monotonic stack's O(n) bound comes entirely from the invariant that no element is ever reconsidered after being popped — every comparison either advances the outer index or permanently retires an element from the stack. Brute force redoes comparisons that the stack version proves are unnecessary, one settled answer at a time.

For genuinely small inputs, brute force's O(1) space and simpler code can still be the right call in practice — the same crossover-point reasoning that applies everywhere else in complexity analysis.

slides.subTitle: Mishandling duplicates
slides.markdown:
The comparison inside the `while` loop — `<` vs `<=`, `<` vs `>` — changes which element "wins" on ties, and getting it backward silently breaks duplicate handling rather than crashing.

For next-greater-element, using `<=` instead of `<` (`while stack and nums[stack[-1]] <= nums[i]`) means equal values also trigger a pop, which is correct if the problem wants the *next strictly greater* element to still count equal values as "not greater" — but wrong if duplicates should be treated as their own next-greater match. There's no universal right answer; it depends on the exact problem statement, which is exactly why this is a common source of off-by-one-feeling bugs that only surface on inputs with repeated values.

The fix is always the same discipline: write out what should happen for two adjacent equal values *before* choosing `<` vs `<=`, rather than guessing and hoping the test cases don't include duplicates.
